Let him cook
LET him KOOK
verb phrase (Gen-Z slang)
From hip-hop and sports slang, where cooking means producing something excellent (a producer cooking up beats in the studio; a basketball player cooking his defender). "Let him cook" — let him keep going, he is onto something — became a widespread Twitter and TikTok reply around 2022–2023, used for an unusual idea, a risky plan, or someone mid-explanation. Note the opposite: he’s cooked means he is finished.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang let him cook means "let him keep going; he is onto something." It is said when someone has a strange idea, an unconventional plan, or a half-finished argument that others want to shout down. At bottom it is a plea for patience before judgment, and Scripture approves the instinct. "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). The best "let him cook" in the Bible came from Gamaliel, when the council wanted to kill the apostles: "Refrain from these men, and let them alone" (Act 5:38), for "if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it" (Act 5:39). The Christian observation is that patience is not the same as approval. Paul says "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21) — let him cook, then taste the dish. Not every idea deserves the stove: when someone starts cooking up sin or false doctrine, the Christian does not wait to see how it turns out. A father tells his son: give people room to finish; hear them out before you mock; and when it is your turn at the stove, cook something you would be glad to serve to the Lord.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (hip-hop and sports cooking; Twitter and TikTok c. 2022–2023) for letting someone continue because he is onto something — Gamaliel’s patience (Act 5:38), held together with Paul’s "Prove all things" (1Th 5:21).

LET HIM COOK, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2022–present; hip-hop and sports origin) Let him continue; he is onto something. "He wants to build a hovercraft for the science fair? Let him cook."

Variants: let her cook, let them cook; he’s cooking, he is doing well; what is he cooking?, what is he up to? Opposite: cooked, finished, doomed.

Plain older sense: to prepare food by heat; figuratively, to cook up a scheme or cook the books (falsify accounts).

Webster (1828), root word cook: “COOK, verb transitive [&hellip;] 1. To prepare, as victuals for the table, by boiling, roasting, baking, broiling, etc. To dress, as meat or vegetables, for eating. 2. To prepare for any purpose. 3. To throw. [&hellip;]”

Decode for parents: a call for patience with an odd idea. Teach your children to hear out, then test.

Key Scripture

Act 5:38 — "And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:"

Act 5:39 — "But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God."

Pro 18:13 — "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."

Jas 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

1Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

Modern Corruption

Let him cook is patience before judgment, which Scripture commends; its only drift is patience without testing — letting someone cook up sin because the idea is bold.

expand to see more

Much of what passes for wit among teenagers is the quick shutdown: a kid offers a strange idea and the room laughs before he finishes the sentence. Let him cook pushes back on that, and rightly. Proverbs calls answering before hearing "folly and shame" (Pro 18:13), and James wants every man "swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). Gamaliel’s counsel saved the apostles’ lives because he was willing to wait and see whether the work was of God (Act 5:38–39).

But wait-and-see is not the whole of wisdom. Some dishes are poison from the first ingredient. When a friend is cooking up a lie, a revenge, a secret relationship, or a novel doctrine, "let him cook" is cowardice dressed as open-mindedness. Paul’s rule holds both halves together: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21). Hear people out; then taste, test, and say no when the dish is bad. Teach your children to be the kind of friend who listens long and judges righteously.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin coquere (to cook) → English cook → hip-hop and sports: cooking, producing something excellent → c. 2022–2023: "let him cook."

Latin coquere — to cook, to ripen; Old English coc, a cook

Figurative English: cook up a plan; cook the books

Hip-hop: producers cooking up beats in the studio

Sports: a player cooking a defender

c. 2022–2023 Twitter / TikTok: "let him cook"; opposite cooked

Usage

""Bro is explaining his plan to start a lawn business at fourteen. Let him cook.""

"Hear before you answer (Pro 18:13)."

"Let him cook, then prove all things (1Th 5:21)."
